title: Governor of Maine

context.text: Open seat: Democratic Gov. Janet Mills is term-limited. Maine has no lieutenant governor, so there are no running mates. Maine uses ranked-choice voting in primaries but not in the governor's general election, so the winner needs only a plurality.

Democratic primary (June 9, 2026): the ranked-choice tabulation went to a final round in which Hannah Pingree won with 56.2% of continuing ballots over Nirav Shah; Troy Jackson, Shenna Bellows and Angus King III were eliminated in earlier rounds.

Republican primary: Bobby Charles led the first round with about 38% in a seven-candidate field and won the nomination through the ranked-choice tabulation; Jonathan Bush, Garrett Mason, Ben Midgley, David Jones, Owen McCarthy and Robert Wessels also ran.

The Secretary of State's certified general-election candidate list shows three candidates for governor: Hannah Pingree (D), Bobby Charles (R) and Rick Bennett, who is on the ballot as an independent. Bennett is a state senator and former chair of the Maine Republican Party who left the party in 2025. Two declared write-in candidates, John Glowa and Randy Wilcox, appear on the Secretary of State's October 15 write-in list.

candidates.name: Hannah Pingree
candidates.currentRole: Former director, Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future (2019–2025); former Speaker of the Maine House

summary.text: Hannah Pingree is the Democratic nominee for governor. She served in the Maine House of Representatives from 2002 to 2010, including as Speaker from 2008 to 2010, and directed Gov. Janet Mills's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 to 2025.

background.text: Grew up on North Haven, Maine; graduated from Brown University with a degree in political science.
Served four terms in the Maine House (2002–2010), chairing the Health and Human Services Committee, serving as Majority Leader (2006–2008) and as Speaker (2008–2010).
Directed the Governor's Office of Policy Innovation and the Future under Gov. Janet Mills from 2019 to 2025.

priorities.text: Affordability agenda 'Maine's Next Chapter': $100 million a year for affordable housing, permitting reform, lower energy bills, and holding utilities accountable.
A public health insurance option, lower prescription drug costs, affordable child care and universal free pre-K.
Property tax relief by doubling the homestead exemption, and further progressive tax reform building on Maine's new millionaire's tax.

positions.summary: Proposes launching a state public health insurance option.
Proposes cutting red tape to speed housing permitting and supporting local zoning reforms that increase density, alongside $100 million a year for affordable housing development.
Proposes building on Maine's new millionaire's tax to advance further progressive tax reform and requiring non-resident second-home owners to pay a fairer share.

record.text: Her campaign says she faced down corporate lobbyists and an all-out campaign from the chemical industry to pass the Kid-Safe Products Act, a law to remove toxic chemicals from everyday toys and clothing. The legislature's text for the related 123rd Legislature law is L.D. 2048, 'An Act To Protect Children's Health and the Environment from Toxic Chemicals in Toys and Children's Products' (Public Law ch. 643).
In the Mills administration, her campaign says she spearheaded the largest pipeline of new housing in production in MaineHousing's 50-year history.

candidates.name: Bobby Charles
candidates.currentRole: Attorney and former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs (2003–2005)

summary.text: Bobby Charles is the Republican nominee for governor. A lawyer who grew up in Wayne, Maine, he served as Assistant Secretary of State for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs from 2003 to 2005 and later founded a consulting firm in Washington, D.C.

background.text: Earned a B.A. from Dartmouth College (1982), an M.A. from Oxford (1984) and a J.D. from Columbia Law School (1987).
Served as U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs, 2003–2005; founded The Charles Group, a consulting firm based in Washington, D.C.

priorities.text: Eliminating Maine's income tax over four years, rolling back mandates on towns and cities and reducing business regulation.
Dismantling the state Department of Health and Human Services, citing the child welfare system.
priorities.quote: I am going to completely dismantle DHHS, from top to bottom,

priorities.text: Returning schools to a focus on outcomes.
priorities.quote: We have to go back to outcomes,

candidates.name: Rick Bennett
candidates.ballotNote: Independent. Maine has no lieutenant governor.

summary.text: Rick Bennett is an independent candidate for governor and a state senator who left the Republican Party in 2025. He previously served in the Maine House (1990–1994) and Senate (1996–2004), was Senate President in 2001–2002, and chaired the Maine Republican Party from 2013 to 2017.

background.text: Elected to the Maine House in 1990; was the Republican nominee for Maine's 2nd Congressional District in 1994 and lost the 2012 Republican U.S. Senate primary.
Served in the Maine Senate from 1996 until term limits in 2004, becoming Senate President in 2001; returned to the Senate in 2020 and has served since.
Chaired the successful ballot initiative banning foreign governments from spending in Maine elections, according to his campaign.

priorities.text: Housing: a state-backed down payment guarantee for first-time buyers and incentives to restart Maine's factory-built housing industry.
priorities.quote: putting Maine on a fast track to build more homes that people can afford in connected communities

priorities.text: Energy: reviewing and lowering the authorized return on equity for investor-owned utilities.
priorities.quote: I will review and lower the authorized return on equity for investor-owned utilities so you’re not overpaying.

priorities.text: Independence from the parties and from special interests.
priorities.quote: As an independent, I answer to Mainers, not party bosses, not special interests, and not the insiders who keep protecting a system that is failing our state.

record.text: Voted yes on accepting the 'ought not to pass' report on L.D. 1134, 'An Act to Prohibit Males from Participating in Female Sports or Using Female Facilities'; the motion passed 21–14.
Voted yes on enactment of L.D. 143, 'An Act to Improve Women's Health and Economic Security by Funding Family Planning Services'; it passed 19–14.
Voted yes on the minority 'ought to pass' report on L.D. 208, 'An Act to Eliminate the 72-hour Waiting Period on Firearm Purchases'; the motion passed 18–17.
Voted yes on the majority 'ought not to pass' report on L.D. 1230, 'An Act to Abolish the 72-hour Waiting Period for a Gun Purchase'; the motion passed 20–15.

Voted yes on the minority 'ought to pass as amended' report on L.D. 1666, which would add the offices of governor, state senator and state representative to ranked-choice voting in general elections; the motion passed 19–13.

researchNotes: The slate was checked against the Maine Secretary of State's certified 2026 General Election Candidates List (Excel, filed 7/27/2026) and the declared write-in list updated 10/15/2026: the only governor candidates are Pingree (D), Charles (R) and Bennett (independent/unenrolled), with write-ins John Glowa and Randy Wilcox. Primary results are from the Wikipedia race article (its first-round figure for Charles is 38.0% in the table and 37.7% in the text, so the guide says about 38%). Ballotpedia blocked automated access. Maine has no lieutenant governor, so there are no running mates. Pingree's record items rest on her campaign's accomplishments page; the guide attributes them to her campaign. The Kid-Safe law text is cited from the legislature's page (L.D. 2048). Charles has never held elected office, so no record items. Bennett's record items are Maine Senate roll calls checked against the official roll-call PDFs; he voted both for L.D. 208 (minority report) and for the L.D. 1230 ought-not-to-pass report, so no gun-law position is inferred. No position is inferred from Bennett's votes alone; they appear only as record items. Charles's website could not be located, so his priorities come from news coverage of his statements; his abortion position was not found. On the 2026-10-19 re-check the Secretary of State files returned HTTP 403 from this machine; the three-candidate slate and the two write-ins were corroborated by The Maine Monitor's governor guide.
